usedLessons.text: Top lesson: Individual skill still wins series, but I overrated one star and ignored the matchup around him: a jungler's edge only counts if his lanes give him something to work with, and POUT showed that a top laner who can win his own lane and take over fights can cancel it. Next time I'll compare the players across all five roles, and when the whole board agrees on one side, I'll take that as a reason to look harder at the other team's best individual, not as comfort. (from Swiss TLAW vs CFO; picked TLAW, actual CFO 1-0)

Top lesson: Individual skill still wins series, but in a Bo1 I have to check whether the star's lane can actually turn that edge into a lead before I treat it as the whole argument. When the opposing team has a proven jungle-support duo that can steal a messy game, I should rate that duo as skill too, not dismiss it as chaos, and I should be more skeptical of a Viper-sized edge when the whole BLG team is the one the crowd is backing. usedLessons.text: Jungle lesson: The early game still decides everything, so I should judge who wins the first fifteen minutes from the jungle matchup, the draft's early pressure and the first-objective setups, not from "better team" or region labels, which only count when the scouting report flags a big gap. When the other jungler can force early skirmishes, like Elyoya on Lee Sin, a Bo1 gives the favorite no time to recover, so I should cut my confidence instead of assuming they'll win tempo by default. (from Swiss BLG vs MKOI; picked BLG, actual MKOI 1-0)

usedLessons.text: Mid lesson: Pool depth only matters if it shows up in the draft, and in a Bo1 a team's few comfort picks (like MKOI's Ryze and Lee Sin) can beat a broader pool, so I should judge how each side's best picks match up instead of counting champions. When the upset path I name is built on the opponent's comfort picks, I should cut my confidence until the draft shows BLG can deny or punish them, and not lean on league strength unless the report flags a big gap. Mid lesson: Pool depth on paper isn't the same as draft leverage; under Fearless, a star's signature comfort picks (POUT's Akali, Viktor, Lucian) can matter more than the number of "comfortable" options a team has. Next time I'll check who actually wins the contested picks and whether the opponent's star can be shut out, rather than assuming breadth beats a few high-impact pools. I also shouldn't lean on region reputation like "shaky against outside teams" unless the report flags a big gap, and should let the draft carry the argument. Vi/Jarvan winning the first skirmishes mattered as much as the Jayce/Gnar scaling puzzle, so I should check whether a comp gets priority and can finish a lead, not just whether it outscales the opposing star. Next time I'll name the specific star-player champion (like POUT's Akali) and the lane-tempo pick that must be denied before I lean on a confident call, and I won't claim the draft explanation proves itself from a single result. ADC lesson: When a Bo1 leans on records, check whether a team's "perfect" stat, like CFO's 5-for-5 on converting leads, is conditional on something the other team's numbers say it rarely gets, and weight it by how often that condition happens. A modest game-record edge (53-46 vs 38-42) paired with early-lead tendencies can justify a slightly firmer lean, but one game still doesn't prove it, so I'll move confidence in small steps rather than jumps. (from Swiss CFO vs MKOI; picked MKOI, actual MKOI 1-0)

Support lesson: I was right about MKOI, but I read the mood from one game and gave chemistry credit for a result that Elyoya's early tempo and the draft also explain. Next time I'll look for team-level evidence that the room is actually working, such as comms, how they recover after setbacks, or roster and coaching stability, and I'll hold my confidence down when all I have is one clean-looking win.
